## Proof

**Problem.** Determine $|X|$ where $X = \{R \subseteq \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N} : R^{*} = \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\}$.

**Upper bound.** Every element of $X$ is a relation on $\mathbb{N}$, i.e., a subset of $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$. Since $|\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}| = \aleph_0$, the total number of relations on $\mathbb{N}$ is $2^{\aleph_0}$. Hence
$$|X| \le 2^{\aleph_0}.$$

**Lower bound.** We construct $2^{\aleph_0}$ distinct elements of $X$.

Define the **backbone** relation
$$B = \{(n,\, n+1) : n \in \mathbb{N}\} \cup \{(n+1,\, n) : n \in \mathbb{N}\}.$$
This is the two-way infinite path on $\mathbb{N}$. We claim $B^{*} = \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ (under either interpretation of $R^{*}$ — reflexive-transitive or purely transitive closure):

- For $a < b$: the path $a \to a+1 \to \cdots \to b$ has length $b - a \ge 1$, so $(a,b) \in B^{+}$.
- For $a > b$: the path $a \to a-1 \to \cdots \to b$ has length $a - b \ge 1$, so $(a,b) \in B^{+}$.
- For $a = b$: the path $a \to a+1 \to a$ has length $2 \ge 1$, so $(a,a) \in B^{+}$.

Thus $B^{+} = \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, and consequently $B^{*} = \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ as well.

Now, $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ and $|\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N} \setminus B| = \aleph_0$ (removing a countable set from a countable set leaves a countable — in particular infinite — set). For **every** subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N} \setminus B$, define
$$R_S = B \cup S.$$
Since $B \subseteq R_S$, we have $B^{*} \subseteq R_S^{*}$, so $R_S^{*} \supseteq \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, hence $R_S^{*} = \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$. Therefore $R_S \in X$ for every $S$.

The map $S \mapsto R_S$ is injective: if $S_1 \ne S_2$, say $(a,b) \in S_1 \setminus S_2$, then $(a,b) \in R_{S_1} \setminus B$ but $(a,b) \notin R_{S_2}$, so $R_{S_1} \ne R_{S_2}$.

The number of subsets $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}\setminus B$ is $2^{\aleph_0}$. Hence
$$|X| \ge 2^{\aleph_0}.$$

**Conclusion.** Combining both bounds,
$$|X| = 2^{\aleph_0}.$$

The cardinality of $X$ is $\boxed{2^{\aleph_0}}$ (the cardinality of the continuum).
